source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Experiment 4: two analogous stories plus a request to describe their similarities beat one analog plus a control story. Schema quality was written down and scored.
numbers: Two similar analogs 39% pre-hint, 79% total (N=28); two dissimilar 52%, 83% (N=23); one analog+control 21%, 53% (N=47). Two vs one: 45% vs 21% pre-hint (G2=6.35, p<.01); 80% vs 53% total (p<.003).
limits: Convergence (radiation) problem only. The control condition also had to compare two unrelated stories, which may have induced a bad schema and hurt. Undergraduates, written protocols.
agent_relevance: Two compared cases are the minimum for induction. Comparing a case to an irrelevant one can do harm, so the case pair must be chosen, not random.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Quality of the induced schema predicts transfer. Good schemas almost always transferred; poor schemas often did not.
numbers: Exp 4 (N=30 usable in the schema table): good schema 91% solved pre-hint (10/11), intermediate 40%, poor 30%; 9 of 30 never solved. Overall only 21% wrote good schemas, 20% intermediate, 59% poor.
quote: the better the schema, the more successful was transfer performance
limits: Correlational. Authors warn that skilled solvers may both write good schemas and transfer well. Cell sizes small.
agent_relevance: Most of the time the comparison step fails to produce the abstraction (59% poor). The agent must check the quality of the induced principle by code (does it cover both cases?) before using it.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Giving a single story plus a stated principle did NOT help transfer. The principle added nothing once a story was present.
numbers: Exp 2 (N=88): analog+principle 32% pre-hint, 80% total (N=31); analog only 29%, 79% (N=28); principle only 28%, 66% (N=29). No significant differences.
limits: The principle was a short verbal statement at the end of the story. Principle-only subjects still beat a 10% base rate, so the statement alone carried some information.
agent_relevance: Telling the model a principle is not the same as inducing one. In one-example prompts an added abstract rule may be ignored.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Spatial diagrams added to one story did not help, but diagrams plus two analogs helped a lot. Aids work when two cases are being compared.
numbers: Exp 3 (N=66): analog+diagram 23% pre-hint, 81% total; analog only 40%, 76%. Exp 6 (N=189): with diagram 57% vs 37% pre-hint (p<.01), 92% vs 79% total (p<.01); similar vs dissimilar pairs made no difference.
limits: Single study. 92% total is near ceiling. Diagram was an abstract arrow picture that subjects also drew.
agent_relevance: An abstract structured representation (a schema template) helps most when attached to a comparison of two cases, not one.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Adding the verbal principle to a pair of analogs DID raise transfer and schema quality, unlike the single-story case.
numbers: Exp 5 (N=143): with principle 62% pre-hint, 82% total; without 40%, 67% (G2=6.75, p<.01; G2=4.34, p<.05). Good schemas 44% with principle vs 10% without; poor 23% vs 60%.
limits: Total gain is modest (15 points). The hint stage is part of the measure.
agent_relevance: A principle is a guide to the mapping, effective when two cases are side by side. Order: cases first, principle as a guide to the comparison.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Surface similarity of the two analogs did not matter (similar-domain pair vs dissimilar pair). Baselines: about 10% solve without any story; about 30% pre-hint and about 75% total with one story.
numbers: Exp 4: 39% vs 52% pre-hint (G2<1). Exp 6: no similar vs dissimilar effect on solution frequency (94/90% with diagrams, 79/79% without).
limits: Null results with modest cell sizes; Exp 4 authors say cell counts were too low to test schema-by-similarity interaction.
agent_relevance: Diverse pairs are not worse than similar pairs for induction in this task, so we need not hunt for near-duplicates.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Direct extension of Gick and Holyoak: comparison helps only when the test is immediate and in the same context. After a context change or one week, pre-hint transfer vanished.
numbers: Exp 1: two-analog compare vs one-analog total 71% vs 41% (p<.01); pre-hint 47% for two-analog compare. Two-analog no-comparison did slightly better than compare in total (74% vs 68%). Exp 2: no condition exceeded the 10% base rate pre-hint after 30 min or one week; hint-aided total 65% (30 min) vs 42% (1 week).
limits: Floor effect in Exp 2 means no conclusion about comparison there. The greater-effort account (more processing, not abstraction) was not ruled out in Exp 1.
agent_relevance: Induced schemas do not fire by themselves in a new context. The agent needs an explicit retrieval step (see analogical access subfield) and cannot rely on the schema being noticed.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Transfer after a context shift and one-week delay became large with three changes together: three source analogs, detailed schema-oriented questions, and a target reworded to cue the shared structure.
numbers: Exp 4 (N=90): directive questions + aquarium problem 36% vs 10% pre-hint (p<.01), 70% vs 42% total. Exp 5 (N=23, one week delay): 3 stories 64%, 2 stories + solved third problem 83% pre-hint; overall 74% pre-hint vs 7% and 23% in earlier one-week conditions. Appropriate schema 81% vs 0% pre-hint (only 2 poor).
quote: spontaneous transfer between small numbers of dissimilar analogs is difficult to obtain, it can be achieved by manipulations that foster abstraction
limits: Exp 5 small groups (11 and 12). Several manipulations changed at once, so each cannot be isolated. The schema effect in Exp 5 rests on 2 poor-schema subjects.
agent_relevance: Recipe: three cases, guided questions about the shared causal features, and restate the new problem in structural terms.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Guided comparison questions raise the rate of good schemas sharply.
numbers: Exp 4: appropriate schemas 86% with the directive questions vs 26% with less directive ones (G2=28.91, p<.0001). Subjects with appropriate schemas: 32% vs 12% pre-hint, 68% vs 39% total.
limits: The scoring rule changed slightly between experiments; the directive questions partly gave away the target features.
agent_relevance: Open-ended 'what is common' prompts yield poor schemas; targeted slot questions work better. The induction operator should ask structured questions (goal, constraint, key mechanism).

source: Thompson, Gentner & Loewenstein (2000) Avoiding missed opportunities in managerial life
finding: Negotiation transfer: comparing two cases to derive a principle gave nearly three times the real transfer of giving advice on each case separately.
numbers: Contingency contracts in the face-to-face negotiation: 14/22 dyads (64%) Comparison vs 5/22 (23%) Advice; chi2(1,N=44)=7.50, p<.01. Contingency contract paid more than compromise: t(42)=2.48, p<.05. Comparison-group average gain was only a nonsignificant trend.
limits: Master of Management students; one principle (contingency contract); 44 dyads. The money result was only a trend.
agent_relevance: Behavioural transfer, not just recall, is raised by forcing a compare-and-derive step. Same two cases, same page, different instruction.

source: Thompson, Gentner & Loewenstein (2000) Avoiding missed opportunities in managerial life
finding: Separate-case reasoning showed no spontaneous comparison, and the quality of case-specific advice was unrelated to later behaviour. The quality of the derived principle did relate.
numbers: No one in Advice referred to case 1 while answering case 2. Dyads advising to take the bet used a contingency contract 25% (2/8) vs 18% (2/11). Comparison: one partner with a good principle 45% (5/11), both partners 88% (7/8), Fisher p=.08. 85% of Advice dyads proposed a better solution than the bet.
limits: The principle-quality link is marginal (p=.08). Small cells.
agent_relevance: Even a good answer to each case does not abstract anything. Do not count correct case-level solutions as evidence of induction.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson & Gentner (2003) Analogical learning in negotiation teams
finding: Follow-up with teams: comparison again beat separate cases, but the margin was smaller and only marginal in the direct test. Separate-case study was no better than no training.
numbers: Contingent contracts: Comparison 24/60 (40%), Separate 8/37 (22%), Baseline 50/213 (23%). Comparison vs Separate chi2(1,N=97)=3.50, p=.06. Three-way chi2(2,N=310)=7.08, p<.05. Expected joint gain $4.76M vs $4.28M vs $4.19M. Schema induced: 21/38 (55%) vs 12/38 (32%), p<.05. Teams 32% vs solo 34%, ns.
limits: The direct comparison vs separate is marginal. The gap (18 points) is smaller than the 41-point gap in the Thompson et al. (2000) study.
agent_relevance: Realistic effect is smaller than first reports. Separate-case exposure is worth about nothing, so adding more examples without comparison should not be expected to help.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson & Gentner (2003) Analogical learning in negotiation teams
finding: Comparison was needed to make people link the cases. Almost nobody connected them when told to analyse them separately.
numbers: All Comparison participants described connections between the two cases; 18% of Separate Cases participants did, and many of those links were weak.
limits: Manipulation check, not an outcome. Same research group as the original.
agent_relevance: Check for our agent: log whether the model actually cites the other case when writing the principle.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge
finding: Late abstraction: comparing two analogous cases at the time of recall made people retrieve a matching earlier case from memory.
numbers: Exp 4 (N=73): recalled the prior analogous example 27% comparison vs 6% separate (chi2=6.12, p<.05); surface-similar example retrieved 30% vs 78%. Exp 1 (N=62 pairs): contingent agreements 59% vs 33% (chi2=4.22, p<.05); 88% vs 17% linked the two cases.
limits: Retrieval stays low in absolute terms (27%). Exp 1 to 3 rely on autobiographical recall, which cannot be fully verified.
agent_relevance: A compared pair acts as a relational probe into memory. Link to the analogical access subfield: induce a schema from the current case plus one remembered case, then query the store with the schema, not the surface text.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009) Reviving inert knowledge
finding: A single schema-abstraction account is reported to capture both backward (retrieval) and forward (transfer) effects in simulation.
numbers: Five experiments plus simulation studies (SME-style model). No further numbers recorded from the simulation.
limits: Hand-coded structured representations; no raw text input.
agent_relevance: Supports implementing induction as alignment of two structured descriptions with a code check, rather than a free-text summary.

source: Kurtz, Miao & Gentner (2001) Learning by analogical bootstrapping
finding: Comparison helps only when it is intensive. Separate interpretation gave no benefit; joint interpretation with listing of correspondences gave the most insight.
numbers: Heat-flow scenarios, 4 conditions, 20 participants each (N=80). Differences listed F(3,76)=2.75, p<.05; causal-relevance rating of descriptions 4.95 (best condition) vs 3.50 (control). 48% of joint-interpretation participants used all three key schema terms vs 23% of non-comparing. Similarity ratings F(3,76)=4.42, p<.05.
limits: Proportion of alignable differences was not significant (F=1.33, p>.10). One domain; coarse ratings.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to consider both cases may be inert. The operator should require an explicit correspondence table (A maps to B).

source: Hattikudur, Sidney & Alibali (2016) Does comparing informal and formal procedures promote mathematics learning?
finding: Boundary condition: comparing informal and formal solution procedures helped conceptual learning only for learners who did not like maths.
numbers: N=111 undergraduates. Conceptual items 2.83 vs 1.49, t(103)=2.5, p=.01; procedural items 3.90 vs 4.40 (ns, comparison slightly lower). Condition by item type t(103)=-2.46, p=.02. Learners who liked maths: no difference. Pretest by condition t(103)=1.82, p=.07.
limits: Attitude was a single self-rating item. Comparison group gained conceptual but not procedural knowledge.
agent_relevance: Comparison adds value where learners would not compare spontaneously. A strong model that already compares internally may gain little from forced comparison; test per task, not by default.

source: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach & Schunn (2011) Aligning structural components across case comparisons (SREE abstract of the meta-analysis)
finding: Meta-analysis of learning by case comparison (conference abstract of the work): a medium effect favouring comparison over other instruction.
numbers: 57 experiments, 336 tests, random effects d = .60 (95% CI .47 to .72); Q(56)=136.74, p<.001, I2=59%. Fail-safe N 2,795 (experiments) and 5,244 (tests).
limits: Abstract only, not the journal paper. A search summary of the published version gave d = .50 for the same 57 experiments, so the figure likely changed; the journal version was not opened. Mixed classroom and lab studies.
agent_relevance: Use d between .5 and .6 as the expectation for comparison-based learning in humans. Not an LLM effect size.

source: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach & Schunn (2011) Aligning structural components across case comparisons (SREE abstract of the meta-analysis)
finding: Moderators: five moderated the effect (content, principle, features, objective, lag). Age, setting, experience and type of comparison task did not.
numbers: 15 moderators coded, kappa .80. Domain, context and dependent-measure effects disappeared once correlated variables were held fixed. Maths, science and other domains were equivalent when the design was brief and learners familiar with the subject.
limits: Direction of each moderator is in tables not shown in the abstract. Few studies with adolescents.
agent_relevance: The comparison benefit held across ages and experience, so it is not only a novice effect. The principle and the objective of the comparison matter more than who learns.

source: Boyce et al. (2023), student replication of Gick and Holyoak 1983, listed in FORRT Replication Atlas
finding: Search summary: a student replication project, classed as successful, found that adding the verbal statement had a clear positive effect on transfer from a pair of analogs.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers.
limits: Single small student project; seen only as a search summary.
agent_relevance: Weak extra support for the Exp 5 result of Gick and Holyoak; do not cite numbers.

source: Replication of Kurtz & Loewenstein (2007), Memory & Cognition (2017)
finding: Search summary: comparing two analogous targets improved transfer over standard transfer; comparing the target with a non-analogous problem did not.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers.
limits: Authors and exact title not confirmed; summary only.
agent_relevance: Matches the Gick and Holyoak finding that an irrelevant partner does no good. The chosen cases must be analogous.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a step back: step-back prompting
finding: Step-back prompting (first ask for the underlying principle, then solve) lifted PaLM-2L on physics, chemistry and temporal knowledge QA.
numbers: PaLM-2L: MMLU Physics 66.4% to 73.2%, Chemistry 70.9% to 81.8%; TimeQA 41.5% to 66.0% (68.7% with retrieval); MuSiQue 35.5% to 42.6%. Zero-shot CoT gave 65.0% and 75.3% on MMLU. Averages over 5 runs, std 0.4 to 3.1.
quote: improves PaLM-2L performance on MMLU (Physics and Chemistry) by 7% and 11% respectively, TimeQA by 27%, and MuSiQue by 7%
limits: Headline numbers are on one model family. GPT-4 + CoT reaches 82.9% on MMLU Physics, above step-back on PaLM-2L (73.2%).
agent_relevance: A cheap one-shot abstraction step helps weaker models on principle-heavy items. Test as a candidate operator against plain at equal tokens (G7).

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a step back: step-back prompting
finding: Step-back gave no gain where the principle is trivial, and one demonstration was enough.
numbers: StrategyQA 82.8% to 82.7% (CoT 83.6%); GSM8K PaLM-2L 75.8% plain, step-back 84.3%, 1-shot 84.5%, CoT 84.4% (equal to simple baselines). More than one exemplar gave no further gain.
limits: The authors' reason (GSM8K principles are too simple) is a hypothesis, not tested.
agent_relevance: Abstraction pays only when the item needs a non-obvious principle. Fire it when plain attempts disagree (G1), not on every item.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a step back: step-back prompting
finding: Error analysis: step-back fixes some baseline errors and creates others; the reasoning step stays the bottleneck.
numbers: MMLU Physics: corrects 20.5% of baseline errors while introducing 11.9% new errors. Reasoning errors dominate the remaining errors, then math errors.
limits: Error annotation done by the authors.
agent_relevance: Net gain is about 8.6 points, but 11.9% of previously right items turned wrong. A code-level check or fallback to the plain answer is needed (G3, G6).

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts
finding: Buffer of Thoughts: distilled reusable thought templates retrieved per problem beat prompting baselines on ten tasks (GPT-4).
numbers: Game of 24: 82.4% vs GPT-4 3.0%, CoT 11.0%, ToT 74.0%; Checkmate-in-One 86.4% vs 36.4% / 32.8% / ToT 49.2%; Geometric Shapes 93.6% vs 52.6% / meta-prompting 78.2%; MGSM 89.2% vs 85.5% CoT; Python Puzzles 52.4% vs 36.3%; Sonnet Writing 80.0% vs 71.2%. Cost about 12% of multi-query methods.
limits: Templates are distilled from the same task families as the tests, so gains are in-family. The authors list low gain on creativity tasks and weak templates when a weaker model builds the buffer. No independent replication seen.
agent_relevance: Template memory is our library idea with measured gains; strong on rule-bound puzzles, small on open tasks. Check for leakage before trusting the numbers.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts
finding: BoT ablations: removing the problem distiller, the meta-buffer or the buffer manager each hurt; without the manager accuracy did not rise as tasks accumulated.
numbers: Figures 7 to 9 (four benchmarks, Llama3-70B and GPT-4). The text states that accuracy with the buffer manager rises across four rounds and without it shows no upward trend. Per-bar values are in figures only.
limits: Values not extractable from text.
agent_relevance: Learning across tasks needs a manager that curates templates; a static store does not improve over time.

source: Hong et al. (2024) Abstraction-of-Thought makes language models better reasoners
finding: Abstraction-of-Thought: training small models on reasoning that states the abstract plan first beat the same data in CoT format.
numbers: 10k-sample ablation, zero-shot BBH average: Llama-3-8B CoT collection 39.7, CoT ablation 46.5, AoT2CoT 43.0, AoT 49.7; Mistral-7B 38.4, 46.0, 46.1, 50.1. Algorithmic tasks: 50.6 vs 45.2 (Llama), 52.1 vs 45.6 (Mistral). NLP tasks: 48.9 vs 47.6, 48.3 vs 46.3. Full 348k AoT Collection: Llama-3-8B-AoT +9.7 over Llama-3-8B-CoT.
limits: Needs finetuning, so not a scaffold. Gain over matched CoT is 3.2 to 4.1 points on average; most of the 9.7 comes from data. Gain is mostly on algorithmic tasks, 1 to 2 points on NLP tasks.
agent_relevance: Abstract first, concrete second gives a few points over matched step-by-step. Supports the order, but not usable as is for a training-free agent.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own relevant examples and knowledge before solving. It helps larger models and not small ones.
numbers: Abstract reports an average gain of +4% over 0-shot and few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench with GPT-3.5-turbo, PaLM 2 and text-davinci-003. With small models (text-curie-001, text-davinci-001) few-shot CoT with labelled or retrieved exemplars beat self-generation; from text-davinci-002 up self-generation won.
limits: Per-row table values were ambiguous after pdf-to-text, so no row-level numbers are recorded. Self-generated examples are not checked for correctness.
agent_relevance: Self-generated cases could serve as the second case for comparison when no store exists, but quality depends on model scale; a verified store is safer for weak models.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Rival and boundary: GPT models solved original letter-string analogies but dropped sharply on counterfactual versions (new alphabet order, symbol sets) that humans handled.
numbers: Humans stayed high on all variants; GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 declined sharply on the counterfactual set (exact values in figures only). Webb et al. (2023) had found GPT-3 above the human average on the original set.
limits: Letter-string domain only; no single headline figure recorded. The best prompt format was used.
agent_relevance: Models may rely on trained-in analogies rather than induced structure. Test any induced schema on perturbed, novel-surface held-out cases (G3).
